text: Winning / losing positions; XOR of piles.

In an impartial game (公平组合游戏) both players have the same moves, they alternate, and whoever cannot move loses. Every position is either winning (some move leads to a losing position) or losing (every move leads to a winning position, or there is no move). Positions with no moves are losing.

Nim: several piles, a move removes any positive number of stones from one pile. The first player wins exactly when the XOR of all pile sizes is non-zero. From a non-zero XOR there is always a move to XOR 0, and from XOR 0 every move makes it non-zero.

Piles 1 1: XOR 0, the first player loses (the second copies every move). Piles 1 0: XOR 1, take the stone (P2197).
Winning move: let x = XOR of all piles; pick a pile a with a ⊕ x < a and reduce it to a ⊕ x (P1247 prints it).
mex of moves; a sum of games XORs its SG values.

The Sprague–Grundy theorem: every impartial position has a Grundy number SG = mex of the SG values of the positions it can move to (mex = smallest non-negative integer not in the set). A position is losing iff SG = 0, and a sum of independent games has SG = XOR of their SG values: every game behaves like a Nim pile of size SG.
So: compute SG for one small game by brute force (memoised mex), then XOR across the independent parts. A Nim pile of size n has SG = n, which is why plain Nim uses the XOR of the sizes.

Subtraction game: from a pile you may remove 1, 3 or 4 stones. SG values for 0, 1, 2, … are 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, … (periodic). Several piles: XOR their SG values. The expected answers here come from an independent Python computation.

A position's SG has at most k + 1 possible values when there are k moves, so the "seen" array only needs size k + 2. Splitting moves (one pile becomes two) give SG = XOR of the parts, inside the mex (分裂游戏
Wythoff, anti-Nim, Euclid's game.

Some games have a formula instead. Wythoff's game (威佐夫博弈): two piles; remove any amount from one pile, or the same amount from both. With a ≤ b, the position is losing exactly when a = ⌊(b − a) · φ⌋, φ = (1 + √5)/2 (P2252).

Anti-Nim (反 Nim, the player taking the last stone loses, P4279): the first player wins iff (all piles are 1 and their number is even) or (some pile is > 1 and the XOR is non-zero). Euclid's game (P1290): whoever first meets a pair with b ≥ 2a can always win.
Losing positions (a, b): (0, 0), (1, 2), (3, 5), (4, 7), (6, 10), … Each difference b − a = 0, 1, 2, 3, … appears exactly once, and a is ⌊difference · φ⌋.

Use long double (or exact integer checks) for φ: with values up to 10⁹ a double can round the wrong way. When no formula is known, compute SG values for small sizes and look for a pattern, then prove or trust it.

Read who loses: in normal play the player who cannot move loses; in "misère" play the player who makes the last move loses, and the XOR rule changes (anti-Nim). Check both small cases by hand before trusting a formula.
